text: Flying in controlled airspace requires prior FAA authorization. Recreational flyers can use LAANC or FAA DroneZone to request authorization. Part 107 remote pilots are subject to 14 CFR 107.41, which prohibits operations in controlled airspace without ATC authorization. Always check whether the airspace class at your location requires authorization before flying.

The FAA UAS Facility Map shows the maximum altitude at which the FAA may authorize UAS operations in controlled airspace around airports. Authorization requests must be at or below the altitude shown for that grid cell. A ceiling of 0 feet means no routine authorization is available for that cell — special coordination with the facility is required. A grid hit is not a clearance; it shows the ceiling up to which you may request authorization.
citation: FAA UAS Facility Map; LAANC authorization process

text: Under 14 CFR 107.51, remote pilots operating under Part 107 may not fly higher than 400 feet above ground level (AGL), except when flying within 400 feet of a structure, where they may fly up to 400 feet above that structure's immediate upper limit. Recreational flyers should stay at or below 400 feet AGL in uncontrolled airspace. Flying higher than 400 feet in controlled airspace requires additional authorization.

A LAANC authorization or FAA DroneZone approval does not allow a flight where a Temporary Flight Restriction (TFR), NOTAM, or stadium restriction also applies. You must check for active TFRs, NOTAMs, and special-event restrictions separately. If any of these are active at your planned flight location and time, the LAANC authorization does not override them.
citation: FAA TFR guidance; 14 CFR 91.137 et seq.; stadium rule under 14 CFR 99.7

text: Under 14 CFR 107.45, no person may operate a small UAS in prohibited or restricted airspace without permission from the using or controlling agency. Prohibited areas (designated with a 'P') have no exceptions for UAS. Restricted areas (designated with an 'R') may allow operations under certain conditions defined by the controlling agency. Always consult official aeronautical charts and check current NOTAM activity.

National Security UAS Flight Restrictions (NSUFRs) are issued as special security instruction TFRs under 14 CFR 99.7. These restrictions protect national security sensitive locations. No UAS operations are permitted in an NSUFR area without prior coordination with the designated facility. Violating an NSUFR can result in interception, use of force, and civil or criminal penalties.

Under 14 CFR 107.51, Part 107 remote pilots must maintain a minimum visibility of 3 statute miles from the control station. They must also maintain at least 500 feet below clouds and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds. Flying in poor visibility or near clouds reduces see-and-avoid ability and increases collision risk with manned aircraft. Always check current weather conditions before and during flight.

Under 14 CFR 107.37, the remote pilot in command of a small UAS must give way to all other aircraft, including manned aircraft and other UAS. You must never fly in a manner that creates a collision hazard. If you see or hear a manned aircraft, land or move away immediately. The right-of-way rules for manned aircraft always apply; UAS do not have right-of-way over any manned aircraft.

A proposed rule for Beyond Visual Line of Sight (BVLOS) operations (sometimes referenced as Part 108) has been under development by the FAA. As of the retrieved date, this rule has NOT been finalized. Existing rules, including the 14 CFR Part 107 visual line of sight requirement, remain in effect. Do not assume BVLOS is permitted based on pending rulemaking. Verify current rule status with the FAA before planning any BVLOS operation.
citation: FAA BVLOS rulemaking (pending as of retrieved date)

text: In May 2026, the FAA proposed new restrictions on UAS operations over fixed-site facilities under Section 2209 authority. As of the retrieved date, this rulemaking is proposed and has NOT entered into force. The existing rules under 14 CFR Part 107 continue to govern UAS operations over such locations. Monitor the FAA docket for updates and verify current status before flying near any potentially affected facility.
citation: FAA Section 2209 proposed rulemaking (May 2026, pending as of retrieved date)
